I doubt I'll be able to see anything, but I want an accurate estimate of whether the Moon is visible right now.

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-10-18 13:17 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-10-18T18:17:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 68.338 degrees and its azimuth is 243.003 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 12.202 degrees and its azimuth is 114.138 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 50.95 percent illuminated, 90.942 degrees from the Sun, and 401155.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data provided, the short answer is: **No, it is extremely unlikely that you will be able to see the Moon with the naked eye.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the astronomical and atmospheric conditions you described:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The primary obstacle is the Sun. You noted the Sun is at an altitude of **68.3°**. This means it is very high in the sky, creating intense atmospheric scattering. Because the Moon is only **12.2°** above the horizon, it is positioned relatively low in the sky. 

In "bright daylight" conditions, the blue light scattered by the atmosphere (Rayleigh scattering) is so intense that it overwhelms the relatively dim reflected light of a 50% illuminated Moon. To see the Moon during the day, it usually needs to be much higher in the sky (closer to the Sun's position) or much closer to a Full Moon phase to provide enough contrast against the blue sky.

### 2. The Phase and Separation
The Moon is **50.95% illuminated** (a First Quarter phase) and is **90.9° away from the Sun**. 
*   Because it is nearly 90 degrees away, it is not "hidden" in the Sun's immediate glare (which would make it impossible to see even with binoculars).
*   However, because it is only half-illuminated, it lacks the "surface area" of light reflection that a Gibbous or Full Moon provides. A Full Moon is much easier to spot during the day because it reflects significantly more light toward your eyes.

### 3. Atmospheric Extinction
At an altitude of only **12.2°**, the Moon's light must travel through a much thicker layer of the Earth's atmosphere than it would if it were overhead. This causes "extinction," where the atmosphere absorbs and scatters the Moon's light before it reaches your eyes. Combined with the high brightness of the midday sun, the Moon's signal is essentially drowned out.

### 4. Human Vision
As an adult with normal unaided eyesight, your pupils will be constricted due to the bright daylight. This further reduces your ability to pick out a faint object (the Moon) against a bright background (the sky).

### Verdict
While the Moon is technically "above the horizon," it will be lost in the brilliance of the day. You might be able to see it if you were looking through **high-powered binoculars or a telescope**, which would allow you to isolate the Moon's disk from the surrounding sky. But with the naked eye in Quito's midday sun, it will remain invisible.
